Q: Test accuracy is greater than training accuracy. What can I do? A:

The other answers are correct in most cases.

But I'd like to offer another perspective. There are specific training regimes that could cause the training data to be harder for the model to learn, for instance, adversarial training or adding Gaussian noise to the training examples.

In these cases, the benign test accuracy could be higher than train accuracy, because benign examples are easier to evaluate. This isn't always a problem, however!

If this applies to you, and the gap between train and test accuracies is larger than you'd like (approximately 30%, as in your question, is a pretty big gap), then this indicates that your model is underfitting to the harder patterns, so you'll need to increase the expressibility of your model. In the case of random forests, this might mean training the trees to a higher depth.

Q: How does getty work with systemd-logind on a linux system? What are their architectures? A:

The explanation needs to touch on so many different things that it ends up being not very linear. I tried my best to make it readable start-to-end, but there is a lot of "side notes".

In short:

  • Getty is the "user interface" for console (tty) logins, but not for any other logins. It is a systemd service, but not really a daemon, as 100% of its functionality is direct user interaction; it does not listen on any sockets.

  • Getty itself provides only half of the "user interface" (the username prompt). After that, intermediate components (namely /sbin/login and PAM) take over to provide the second half (the password prompt) as well as to start your shell.

  • Systemd-logind is a "session registry" for all login types. It is a systemd service, and a daemon which listens for calls over D-Bus.

  • There are two different interactions between them.

  • The main interaction with systemd-logind (session registry) isn't actually performed by getty directly, but through the aforementioned intermediate components (/sbin/login and PAM).

  • The other interaction (on-demand getty start) is more directly between getty and systemd-logind, but is a minor "frill" – so minor as to be largely irrelevant.

In long:

Getty is the program that displays a login prompt on 'tty' lines (both local console such as tty1 and serial ports such as ttyS0).

Getty isn't a daemon, strictly speaking, because it does not listen on any socket addresses for requests – instead it directly interacts with the user by outputting text through /dev/tty* and reading your input.

Traditionally, an instance of getty is started at boot time, for each tty device that is supposed to provide a console login. On Linux before systemd, this was typically done through /etc/inittab, enumerating however many local ttys you wanted to have, plus serial port ttys. In systemd the same is done using multiple instances of getty@.service, e.g. getty@tty1.service.

Getty could be considered your "user interface" for console-based logins, although it does not handle logins to the end. Its job is only to initialize the tty device and display just the initial greeting (the "Username:" prompt, plus a banner from /etc/issue). After you enter the username, the following password prompt isn't from getty itself anymore, but from the /sbin/login program which getty starts on the same tty. That /sbin/login process (not to be confused with systemd-logind!) is what handles prompting for passwords or tokens, password checking (via PAM), and starting the user's shell.

So the user interface of a console login consists of the chain: getty → /sbin/login → your login shell.

Getty is purely for text-based logins on "fixed" or "permanent" tty devices, and is not used for other login types. SSH logins work differently (the sshd daemon handles authentication and only then allocates a transient pty device, so there is nothing for getty to do). Graphical modes have a "display manager" such as GDM or LightDM which entirely replaces getty by displaying a graphical login screen.

Getty itself has only very minor interaction with systemd-logind. Instead of pre-starting all gettys on tty1–tty6 during boot as used to be the tradition, there is a minor feature within logind to detect which console tty is "active" and start the corresponding getty@<tty>.service on demand. (However, tty1 still has a getty started at boot time for robustness. Serial ports also still have their gettys permanently running from boot time, like before.) The behavior of getty doesn't change regardless of when or how it gets started.

(Traditionally, getty instances were pre-started on tty1–tty6 at boot time, so those ttys were permanently allocated for console logins, while graphical (Xorg) sessions would claim tty7 onwards. Switching to "on-demand" gettys on tty2–tty6 allows GDM or LightDM to use tty2 onwards, which I suppose makes it more convenient to switch sessions using Ctrl-Alt-Fx keys. It's a relatively minor feature, really.)

The major interaction with systemd-logind is in the /sbin/login process. After /sbin/login has called PAM to do password checking and user authorization, it calls PAM again with pam_open_session() which in turn calls the various pam_*.so modules to do various arbitrary "new session initialization" procedures. One such module displays your /etc/motd; another module sets up SELinux if necessary; finally the pam_systemd.so module contacts the systemd-logind service over D-Bus in order to "register a session". This happens immediately before /sbin/login starts your shell.

To make things clear, though: There is no direct relationship between /sbin/login and systemd-logind. They only happen to have similar names, but otherwise they are entirely independent components, and /sbin/login can still operate without calling systemd-logind.

And vice versa, systemd-logind is called not only by /sbin/login, but also by sshd, gdm, lightdm, and so on. This is all done through PAM – all these programs use PAM for password checking, and they all call PAM for session initialization, and therefore, they all invoke systemd-logind through pam_systemd.so.

Despite its name, the main purpose of systemd-logind is not really to "perform logins", but only to act as a "session registry" – much like its predecessor ConsoleKit, logind provides a way to associate each user process with a discrete 'session' and a 'display' (tty or graphical).

The main consumers of logind's session data are polkitd (PolicyKit) and udev, which grant various permissions to "local" and/or "active" sessions. For example, when logind notes that tty3 is now active, udev uses that to dynamically grant access to /dev/snd to whichever user is logged in on tty3. Various parts of a graphical desktop interact with system daemons which use PolicyKit to check authorization; e.g. the UDisks service receives 'mount USB stick' calls via D-Bus, and either allows or denies it depending on whether the call came from an "active session && local session" process.

The specific way logind implements "sessions" is by placing processes in Linux 'cgroups' which has evolved into a whole feature on its own – at some point in systemd's lifetime, those cgroups became configurable as "slice" units with resource control – but the original goal was just to have the cgroup name act as a session identifier that unprivileged processes could neither fake, nor escape.

(Earlier, ConsoleKit used to act as the "session registry", but since cgroups weren't a common feature, it worked by providing an unique 'cookie' environment variable to /sbin/login or to GDM, which was inherited by your shell.)

The whole thing – getty, /sbin/login, etc – can still work without systemd-logind. "Session registry" is a secondary function that more-or-less gets involved only after the user has logged in, and is largely useless outside local graphical sessions (often disabled on headless servers). Non-systemd distributions might have seatd to handle device access, or simply not have a session registry at all, relying on traditional statically configured permissions (e.g. access to /dev controlled by manual group membership).

Q: python - how can I generate a WAV file with beeps? A: 
import numpy as np
import wave

# Параметры звука
sample_rate = 44100
duration = 8.0  # Длина бита в секундах
bpm = 95
beat_len = 60 / bpm

def generate_phonk_beat():
    t = np.linspace(0, duration, int(sample_rate * duration), False)
    audio = np.zeros_like(t)

    # Функции инструментов
    def get_kick(t_loc): # Тяжелая бочка
        return np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50 * (1 - t_loc * 2.5) * t_loc) * np.exp(-12 * t_loc)
    
    def get_snare(t_loc): # Грязный хлопок
        noise = np.random.uniform(-1, 1, len(t_loc))
        return noise * np.exp(-20 * t_loc) * 0.4

    def get_hat(t_loc): # Короткий хэт
        return np.random.uniform(-1, 1, len(t_loc)) * np.exp(-60 * t_loc) * 0.1

    # Накладываем ритм на 4 такта
    for i in range(16):
        start = int(i * beat_len * sample_rate)
        chunk = int(beat_len * sample_rate)
        t_loc = np.linspace(0, beat_len, chunk, False)

        # Ритмический рисунок
        if i % 4 == 0 or i % 4 == 2.5: # Kick
            audio[start:start+chunk] += get_kick(t_loc)
        if i % 4 == 2: # Snare
            audio[start:start+chunk] += get_snare(t_loc)
        # Быстрые хэты
        h_chunk = chunk // 2
        audio[start:start+h_chunk] += get_hat(t_loc[:h_chunk])
        audio[start+h_chunk:start+chunk] += get_hat(t_loc[h_chunk:])

    # Нормализация и сохранение
    audio = (audio / np.max(np.abs(audio)) * 32767).astype(np.int16)
    with wave.open('phonk_beat.wav', 'w') as f:
        f.setnchannels(1)
        f.setsampwidth(2)
        f.setframerate(sample_rate)
        f.writeframes(audio.tobytes())

generate_phonk_beat()
print("Файл phonk_beat.wav создан!")

Q: How to detect *every* kind of error when printing to a file, including missing write permissions? A:

Hopefully, weasyprint exits with an error code if it can't write to the file you specified as its output.

Assuming it does, what you should do is check the value of $? immediately after you close the pipe. If it has a non-zero value, then weasyprint is signalling failure.
